contradictions.question: On what day did the temple burn?
contradictions.summary: Both 2 Kings 25:8-9 and Jeremiah 52:12-13 are describing the same event — Nebuzaradan torching Solomon's temple in the fifth month of Nebuchadnezzar's nineteenth year. The problem is the date. Kings puts it on the seventh of the month. Jeremiah puts it on the tenth. Same fire, same year, two different days.
contradictions.commentary:
This is one of those tidy little contradictions that exposes how the Hebrew Bible was actually transmitted. Jeremiah 52 is widely understood by critical scholars to be a near-duplicate of 2 Kings 24-25, lifted into the Jeremiah scroll as an appendix. So when two passages that are supposed to be reproducing the same source disagree on a date, the simplest explanation is a copyist error somewhere in the transmission chain.

The apologist playbook for this one is well-worn. Gleason Archer's go-to move is to suggest that the burning lasted multiple days — Nebuzaradan arrived on the seventh, and the fire actually consumed the building by the tenth, so both dates are "correct." That is of course a subjective opinion on the evidence. The texts themselves don't say that. 2 Kings 25:8 says Nebuzaradan "came" on the seventh and burned the house of the Lord; Jeremiah 52:12 says he "came" on the tenth and burned the house. The verb is the same. The day is different. Reading multi-day arson into one verse to rescue the other is post-hoc rationalization.

The critical consensus, going back to Bernhard Duhm and reflected in modern critical editions, is that this is a scribal variant. Mordechai Cogan and Hayim Tadmor in the Anchor Bible II Kings note that the Lucianic recension of the Septuagint reads "ninth" in 2 Kings 25:8, which suggests the textual tradition itself didn't know which day it was. The Syriac Peshitta on Jeremiah 52:12 reads "seventh," splitting the difference the other way. When ancient translators are pulling the date in opposite directions to harmonize, it's a strong signal that the underlying Hebrew was already corrupt.

The verdict is straightforward. Two passages, drawn from the same source material, disagree on a basic date. The harmonization requires inventing a multi-day burning event that neither text describes. Take your pick — either the texts are inerrant and you have to wave away the disagreement with creative chronology, or the texts are humanly transmitted documents with the same kind of small scribal divergences you find in any ancient manuscript tradition. The second option fits the actual textual evidence.

contradictions.question: How high was the chapiter?
contradictions.summary: The "chapiter" is the ornamental capital on top of the bronze pillars Jachin and Boaz that stood in front of Solomon's temple. Jeremiah 52:22 gives the height as five cubits. 2 Kings 25:17 gives it as three cubits. Same architectural feature, two different measurements, in passages otherwise telling the same story about the Babylonian sack of Jerusalem.
contradictions.commentary:
This is part of a cluster of disagreements between 2 Kings 25 and Jeremiah 52, which are essentially parallel accounts of the fall of Jerusalem. When two passages duplicate each other almost verbatim and then diverge on a specific number, the simplest explanation is textual corruption in one of them. The question is which one preserves the older reading.

The apologist move here, deployed by Archer and others, is to argue that the three-cubit measurement in 2 Kings refers only to the ornamental molding at the very top, while the five-cubit measurement in Jeremiah captures the full capital. Walter Kaiser proposes essentially the same thing — that we're measuring different architectural sub-components. The problem is that both texts use the same Hebrew term — kothereth ("capital") — and both give it as a single height measurement. There's no textual signal that one is measuring a subsection and the other is measuring the whole. You have to import that distinction from outside the text to make the harmonization work.

The critical scholarship — Cogan and Tadmor in the Anchor Bible II Kings, and Lundbom in Jeremiah 37-52 — treats this as a straightforward scribal variant. 1 Kings 7:16 independently gives the height of the chapiter as five cubits, which matches Jeremiah and conflicts with 2 Kings. That's a strong tell. When the parallel description in Kings itself contradicts the later Kings passage on the same number, the most parsimonious explanation is that a scribe somewhere along the way miscopied a numeral. Hebrew numerals in the Iron Age were genuinely ambiguous, and the Septuagint of 2 Kings 25:17 actually preserves "three" as well, suggesting the corruption is old.

The verdict here is the same as the burning-of-the-temple contradiction. Two parallel accounts, one disagrees with the other on a basic number, and the disagreement is internal to Kings itself (1 Kings 7:16 vs. 2 Kings 25:17). That is the signature of textual transmission, not divine dictation. Harmonizing requires inventing architectural sub-components that the text never mentions. It's an ad hoc fix for an obvious copyist error.

contradictions.question: How many men were in the king's presence?
contradictions.summary: 2 Kings 25:18-19 says Nebuzaradan rounded up five men from the king's personal retinue. Jeremiah 52:24-25 — telling the exact same scene — says seven. Same captain of the guard, same priests, same officers, just two different counts of the royal attendants taken into custody.
contradictions.commentary:
This is the third numerical disagreement in a tight cluster of parallel passages describing the fall of Jerusalem, and at this point the pattern is doing the apologists' work against them. If 2 Kings 25 and Jeremiah 52 are independent inerrant records, they should agree on basic head counts. They keep failing to do so.

The standard harmonization, advanced by Archer and echoed by John Haley in his nineteenth-century classic Alleged Discrepancies of the Bible, is to argue that two more men were apprehended elsewhere and added to the list in Jeremiah, while the five in Kings only counts those caught "in the city." That is of course a subjective opinion on the evidence — both texts use the exact same phrase, "in the city," and both describe the men as having been "in the king's presence" or "near the king's person." There is no textual signal that two of them were caught somewhere else. The harmonization invents a distinction the texts do not make. It's a classic post-hoc fix.

The critical view, going back to Bernhard Duhm and reflected in Cogan-Tadmor's Anchor Bible commentary, is that this is once again a scribal variant in the transmission. Lundbom's Anchor Bible Jeremiah 37-52 notes that the Septuagint of Jeremiah 52:25 reads "seven" matching the MT, but the parallel Septuagint of 2 Kings 25:19 reads "five" matching its MT — meaning the divergence is old, predating the Greek translation. That's exactly what you would expect if one Hebrew exemplar had been corrupted before the LXX translators got to it. The numbers in Hebrew look very similar in paleo-Hebrew script, and number variants are among the most common scribal errors in the Hebrew Bible.

The verdict is that this is the same kind of error you find in any ancient text with a long transmission history. The harmonization works only by adding details the text doesn't include. If you're committed to inerrancy you'll take that trade. If you're not, you'll see what the evidence is actually showing: two scribes, two different numbers, both copied forward into the canon.

contradictions.question: On what day of the month was Jehoiachin released from prison?
contradictions.summary: 2 Kings 25:27 says Evil-Merodach released Jehoiachin on the twenty-seventh day of the twelfth month. Jeremiah 52:31 — telling the same story — says it was the twenty-fifth day. Same king, same prison, same release event, two different dates two days apart.
contradictions.commentary:
This is the fourth numerical contradiction in the parallel material between 2 Kings 24-25 and Jeremiah 52. At this point we are looking at a systemic pattern rather than a single fluke. The story of Jehoiachin's release is verbatim near-duplicate text in both books, and the only thing they cannot agree on is the calendar date.

The go-to apologist response is the multi-day-event move again. Archer suggests the proclamation was issued on the twenty-fifth and Jehoiachin physically left the prison on the twenty-seventh. Walter Kaiser proposes essentially the same. That is of course a subjective opinion on the evidence. The texts themselves give a single date for the release. 2 Kings says "Evil-Merodach... lifted up the head of Jehoiachin... out of prison" on the twenty-seventh; Jeremiah uses the same verbal construction (nasaʼ et-rosh, idiomatic for granting amnesty) on the twenty-fifth. Both texts are describing the moment of legal release. Inventing a two-day administrative gap is not in the text — it is in the apologist's imagination.

The critical scholarship, including Cogan and Tadmor in Anchor Bible II Kings and Lundbom in Anchor Bible Jeremiah 37-52, accepts this straightforwardly as a textual variant. The Lucianic LXX of 2 Kings 25:27 actually preserves "twenty-fifth," agreeing with Jeremiah, which suggests the variant arose within the Hebrew transmission of Kings itself. William Schniedewind has noted that Jeremiah 52 functions as a deliberate appendix lifted from the Deuteronomistic History, and the small numerical drift between the two versions is exactly the kind of data we'd expect when a passage gets copied between scrolls maintained by different scribal schools.

The verdict is identical to the rest of this cluster. The harmonization requires inventing administrative details the text never mentions. The critical reading recognizes a scribal variant in a manuscript tradition that we can actually track through the Septuagint witnesses. It's not a deep mystery. It's how ancient texts get copied.

contradictions.question: What were the generations from David to the Babylonian Captivity?
contradictions.summary: 1 Chronicles 3:1-16 lists eighteen generations of Judahite kings between David and Jeconiah, the king carried off to Babylon. Matthew 1:6-11 lists fourteen, and Matthew 1:17 explicitly insists there were fourteen "generations from David until the carrying away into Babylon." The two genealogies cover the same dynastic line, and they cannot both be right.
contradictions.commentary:
Matthew is not being subtle here. The author drops fourteen-generation summary statements in Matthew 1:17 as if it's a numerological feature, not a bug. The problem is that the Chronicler — working from royal records, not theological symmetry — knows there were more kings than that. Matthew omits Ahaziah, Joash, Amaziah, and Jehoiakim from the lineup. Four names. Gone.

The traditional apologetic response, going back at least to Eusebius and codified by Archer and Blomberg, is that biblical genealogies often "telescope" — skipping generations is normal in ancient genealogical convention, and "begat" doesn't have to mean direct father-son descent. That is actually true as a general claim about ancient genealogies. The problem is that it doesn't rescue Matthew, because Matthew explicitly counts the generations and announces a specific number. Matthew 1:17 isn't just telescoping silently — it's making a numerical claim. "All the generations from David until the carrying away into Babylon are fourteen generations." Either there were fourteen, in which case the Chronicler is wrong, or there were more and Matthew's count is rhetorical rather than factual.

The critical consensus, articulated by W. D. Davies and Dale Allison in their ICC commentary on Matthew, is that the fourteen-generation scheme is theological numerology, not historiography. Fourteen is the gematria value of David's name in Hebrew (D-V-D = 4+6+4 = 14), and Matthew is structuring the entire genealogy around it. To hit three sets of fourteen, the author had to drop four kings out of the Davidic line. Raymond Brown in The Birth of the Messiah works through this carefully and concludes that Matthew has deliberately compressed the list for symbolic reasons. The Chronicler's list, drawn from older annalistic sources, is the historically intact one.

The verdict is that the contradiction is real but tells us something interesting. Matthew is not trying to give you a registry-office genealogy; he's constructing a theological structure that signals "this is the son of David" through a Hebrew letter-counting trick. The Chronicler, less interested in symbolism, preserved the longer list. You can call this harmonization-by-genre-distinction if you like — but you cannot call both lists historically accurate, and Matthew himself frames his count as historical.

contradictions.question: Was Jechoniah the son or the grandson of Josiah?
contradictions.summary: Matthew 1:11 says "Josias begat Jechonias" — making Jeconiah the direct son of Josiah. 1 Chronicles 3:15-16 says Josiah's sons were Johanan, Jehoiakim, Zedekiah, and Shallum, and then names Jeconiah as the son of Jehoiakim — making him Josiah's grandson, not his son.
contradictions.commentary:
This is collateral damage from Matthew's fourteen-generation scheme. To hit his magic numerological count, Matthew had to drop Jehoiakim out of the list, which collapses two generations into one. The Chronicler, working from the actual royal records, knows that Josiah's son was Jehoiakim and Jehoiakim's son was Jeconiah (also called Coniah and Jehoiachin). Matthew telescoped the line and ended up with Josiah "begetting" his own grandson.

The apologist response, advanced by Archer and others, is that "begat" in biblical Hebrew/Greek genealogies often spans multiple generations and just means "was the ancestor of." That is true in principle. The problem, again, is Matthew 1:17's explicit count of fourteen generations. If "begat" can mean "grandfathered," then the count is meaningless — you can collapse any number of intermediate ancestors and still hit fourteen. But Matthew is making a generational claim, not just an ancestral one. The other apologetic move is to argue that some manuscripts of Matthew 1:11 originally read "Josias begat Jehoiakim, and Jehoiakim begat Jechonias." Bruce Metzger's textual commentary on the Greek New Testament confirms that a small minority of late manuscripts do contain a Jehoiakim reading, but Metzger and the UBS committee judge this an intentional scribal correction, not the original reading. The original Matthew omitted Jehoiakim.

Davies and Allison in the ICC volume on Matthew take this as evidence that Matthew is working from a written genealogical source and editing it for symbolic purposes. Raymond Brown in The Birth of the Messiah goes further and notes that Matthew's genealogy carries multiple compression points, including this one. The author is not pretending to give you a Form 1040 family tree. He's giving you a theological structure with David's name encoded into the counting.

The verdict is that calling Jeconiah Josiah's "son" is an artifact of Matthew's editing, not a separate historical claim. The Chronicler preserves the actual generational structure. The contradiction is real on the surface and only dissolves if you let "begat" mean whatever you need it to mean — at which point you've also given up on the fourteen-generation count being a literal count.

contradictions.question: Was Jeconiah childless?
contradictions.summary: Jeremiah 22:28-30 records Yahweh telling the prophet to "write this man childless" — Jeconiah, king of Judah, will leave no descendant on the throne of David. 1 Chronicles 3:17-18 then lists eight sons of Jeconiah, and Matthew 1:11-16 carries the Davidic line through Jeconiah down to Jesus himself. So Jeconiah is either a childless dead-end or the ancestor of the Messiah, depending on which book you trust.
contradictions.commentary:
The apologist harmonization on this one is well-rehearsed. Archer, Kaiser, and others argue that Jeremiah's "childless" doesn't actually mean biologically childless — it's a juridical pronouncement that no son of Jeconiah will succeed him on the throne. The full text of Jeremiah 22:30 does qualify the curse: "no man of his seed shall prosper, sitting upon the throne of David, and ruling any more in Judah." That is a fair reading of the second half of the verse. The first half, "write this man childless," is the trickier part. The Hebrew ʿariri can mean either literally childless or legally heirless — and the apologetic case leans hard on the second meaning.

The critical scholarship, including Lundbom in Anchor Bible Jeremiah 21-36 and Holladay in Hermeneia Jeremiah Vol. 1, accepts that ʿariri here likely carries a dynastic sense rather than a biological one. So far, this looks like a recoverable harmonization. The problem is that it creates a new problem for Matthew. Because Matthew's whole point of running the genealogy through Jeconiah is to establish Jesus' legal claim to the Davidic throne. If Jeremiah 22:30 explicitly says no descendant of Jeconiah will sit on the throne of David, and Matthew is arguing that Jesus inherits the throne of David through Jeconiah, then Matthew is running directly into the curse the apologists just invoked to save Jeremiah. Raymond Brown notes this in The Birth of the Messiah and observes that some early Christian commentators were aware of the difficulty — which is part of why Luke's genealogy (Luke 3:23-31) avoids Jeconiah entirely and traces Jesus through a different Davidic line via Nathan rather than Solomon.

The verdict is a forced choice. If you read Jeremiah literally — "childless" means without children — it contradicts 1 Chronicles 3:17 outright. If you read it dynastically — no son on the throne — you've rescued the Chronicles list but you've poisoned Matthew's whole genealogical argument. Take your pick. The critical reading is that Jeremiah 22 is a piece of seventh-century-BCE political rhetoric aimed at delegitimizing Jeconiah's line, written before anyone needed to harmonize it with a Christian Messiah, and the contradiction is what happens when later writers try to claim the throne the prophet just cursed.

contradictions.question: Who was Zerubbabel's father?
contradictions.summary: 1 Chronicles 3:19 names Zerubbabel's father as Pedaiah. Ezra 3:2, Nehemiah 12:1, Haggai 1:1, Matthew 1:12, and Luke 3:27 all name him as Shealtiel. That's one tradition against five, naming two different fathers for the same well-known post-exilic Persian-period governor of Judah.
contradictions.commentary:
Zerubbabel is one of the few biblical figures who shows up cleanly in non-biblical Persian-period administrative records. He matters because he's the descendant of David who leads the return from exile and re-establishes worship in Jerusalem. So naturally the Bible cannot agree on who his father was.

The go-to apologist solution is the levirate marriage move. The idea, developed in detail by Eusebius and revived by Archer, is that Shealtiel died without a biological son, so his brother Pedaiah married his widow under Deuteronomy 25:5-10, and the resulting child was legally Shealtiel's heir while biologically Pedaiah's son. The Chronicler reports the biological father; everyone else reports the legal father. That is at least an internally coherent harmonization, and the levirate law is real Israelite custom. The problem is that there is no textual evidence for it. Nothing in 1 Chronicles 3 says Shealtiel died childless, nothing says Pedaiah married his widow, and the surrounding context of 1 Chronicles 3:17-19 gives no hint that the unusual Pedaiah patronymic for Zerubbabel is being explained by a levirate scenario. The harmonization invents facts to fix a discrepancy.

The critical reading, found in Knoppers' Anchor Bible 1 Chronicles 1-9 and in Hugh Williamson's older New Century Bible Commentary on Chronicles, treats this as straightforward genealogical confusion in the post-exilic period. Pedaiah and Shealtiel were brothers, both sons of Jeconiah, and traditions about which one fathered Zerubbabel diverged in the textual record. The Septuagint of 1 Chronicles 3:19 actually reads "sons of Salathiel: Zerubbabel," agreeing with Ezra/Nehemiah/Haggai/Matthew/Luke against the Masoretic Text of Chronicles. That's strong evidence that the Hebrew of Chronicles was corrupted — or that the Chronicler had a different source tradition than the other writers. Either way, it's a transmission problem, not divinely consistent history.

The verdict is that we have a genuine disagreement in the sources, and the levirate harmonization is an apologist invention with zero textual support. The cleanest critical reading is that Pedaiah and Shealtiel were both candidates in the genealogical memory of post-exilic Judah, and the Chronicler preserved one tradition while the rest of the canon preserved the other. That is what messy human transmission of family records looks like.

contradictions.question: Who were the sons of Benjamin?
contradictions.summary: Four biblical lists of Benjamin's sons give four mutually incompatible rosters. Genesis 46:21 names ten sons. Numbers 26:38-40 names five (and demotes two of Genesis' "sons" to grandsons). 1 Chronicles 7:6 says explicitly there were three. 1 Chronicles 8:1-2 then gives yet another list of five — overlapping with but not matching the Numbers list. Four lists, four different answers.
contradictions.commentary:
This is one of the clearest examples of how the Hebrew Bible accumulated multiple, mutually inconsistent tribal genealogies that no later editor bothered to reconcile. Benjamin is supposed to be one of the twelve foundational patriarchs of Israel. You would expect the basic question "who were his sons" to have a single canonical answer. It does not.

The traditional apologetic harmonization, advanced by Archer and worked through in detail by Keil and Delitzsch in their nineteenth-century commentary on Chronicles, is that the lists are partial — each one only names selected sons, and some entries are alternate names for the same person, while others are grandsons being counted as sons in the looser ancient Near Eastern sense. There is something to this. "Ehi" in Genesis 46:21 may be a shortened form of "Ahiram" in Numbers 26:38, and "Muppim/Huppim" may correspond to "Shupham/Hupham." Name corruption across genealogical lists is real. The problem is the explicit count in 1 Chronicles 7:6 — "the sons of Benjamin: Bela, Becher, and Jediael — three." The Chronicler is counting. He says three. And then the very next chapter, in 1 Chronicles 8:1-2, the same author lists five sons with different names — Bela, Ashbel, Aharah, Nohah, Rapha. Not three, not the same names. Within the same book, in consecutive chapters, the count and the names don't match.

The critical scholarship, including Knoppers' Anchor Bible 1 Chronicles 1-9 and Sara Japhet's OTL Chronicles commentary, treats these lists as compilations from different tribal source documents — likely military census lists from different periods, plus genealogical traditions of varying age. Knoppers notes that 1 Chronicles 7 and 1 Chronicles 8 almost certainly draw on different underlying sources, and the Chronicler has stitched them together without harmonizing them. Some scholars have argued that 1 Chronicles 7:6 is actually a damaged list referring to Zebulun rather than Benjamin (the geographic context in chapter 7 supports this), which would partially explain why it doesn't match chapter 8. That is a textual-critical fix, not an inerrancy rescue.

The verdict is that this is what tribal genealogies look like when you compile them across centuries from multiple oral and written sources. The harmonizations work for some name discrepancies but cannot reconcile the explicit count of "three" in 1 Chronicles 7:6 with the five-name list in 1 Chronicles 8:1-2 — let alone with the ten of Genesis 46. Four different traditions, all preserved in the canon, all preserved together as if they did not contradict each other. They do.

contradictions.question: How many men did the chief of David's captains kill?
contradictions.summary: 2 Samuel 23:8 says the chief of David's mighty men raised his spear against eight hundred men and killed them all in one encounter. 1 Chronicles 11:11 — telling the same story, listing the same hero — says three hundred. Same event, same warrior, two different body counts five hundred men apart.
contradictions.commentary:
Even the warrior's name disagrees across the two passages. 2 Samuel 23:8 in the Masoretic Text calls him "Josheb-basshebeth a Tahchemonite," while 1 Chronicles 11:11 calls him "Jashobeam, an Hachmonite." The 2 Samuel reading is widely recognized as corrupt — Josheb-basshebeth is probably a copyist's accidental duplication, and Jashobeam is the original name. So we already know one of these passages has scribal damage. The question is whether the number disagreement is the same kind of damage.

The Archer-style apologetic harmonization is that there were two separate incidents — Jashobeam killed three hundred on one occasion and eight hundred on another, and the two passages are recording different battles. That is of course a subjective opinion on the evidence. Both texts use "at one time" to specify a single encounter, and both are giving the same numerical claim about the same warrior's most famous feat. The two-battle theory is invented to dissolve the contradiction. P. Kyle McCarter's Anchor Bible 2 Samuel commentary and Tsumura's NICOT 2 Samuel both treat this as a single tradition with a textual variant.

The critical reading is that the number in one of these passages has been corrupted in transmission, and the most likely culprit is 2 Samuel. McCarter notes that the Hebrew of 2 Samuel 23 is notoriously rough — the Lucianic Septuagint and 4QSamuela from the Dead Sea Scrolls preserve readings here that diverge significantly from the MT. Anneli Aejmelaeus has done extensive work showing that the Greek tradition of Samuel often preserves an older Hebrew Vorlage than the MT, and the Samuel text we have in our Bibles is one of the most textually unstable books of the Hebrew Bible. The number eight hundred in 2 Samuel 23:8 may itself be a scribal expansion, or three hundred in 1 Chronicles may be the Chronicler smoothing a number he found extravagant. Either way, it's a transmission issue.

The verdict is that this is the same pattern as the Kings/Jeremiah parallels: two manuscripts of the same tradition disagreeing on a number. The two-battles harmonization invents events the text does not describe. The textual-critical reading recognizes ordinary scribal variation in a notoriously rough Hebrew text. Take your pick.

contradictions.question: Who tempted David to number Israel?
contradictions.summary: 2 Samuel 24:1 is unambiguous: "the anger of the Lord was kindled against Israel, and he moved David against them to say, Go, number Israel and Judah." Yahweh himself incites the census. 1 Chronicles 21:1 — telling the exact same story — says "Satan stood up against Israel, and provoked David to number Israel." Same census, same king, same divine motivation, but the agent has been swapped from God to Satan.
contradictions.commentary:
This is one of the most theologically important contradictions in the Hebrew Bible, because it preserves a snapshot of an evolving Israelite cosmology in real time. The Deuteronomist who wrote 2 Samuel has no problem with Yahweh being the direct cause of evil acts. Yahweh hardens Pharaoh's heart, sends evil spirits, kills the firstborn — that is just how monotheism worked in the early period. The Chronicler, writing several centuries later in the post-exilic period, is uncomfortable with this. He has absorbed influences from Persian dualism, where evil has its own agent (Angra Mainyu / Satan-figure), and Second Temple Judaism is developing an increasingly elaborate angelology and demonology. So when the Chronicler reuses the Samuel narrative, he literally swaps out the divine agent.

The traditional apologetic harmonization, advanced by Archer and Walter Kaiser, is that God permitted Satan to incite David, so both passages are technically correct — God is the ultimate cause, Satan is the proximate cause. The texts simply emphasize different aspects of the same causal chain. That is of course a subjective opinion on the evidence. Job 1-2 is sometimes cited as the template — there Yahweh permits the satan to test Job. The problem is that 2 Samuel 24:1 does not say God permitted anything. It says God did it. "He moved David." Active verb. Direct agency. The harmonization works only by importing a doctrine of secondary causation that the Hebrew text never mentions.

The critical reading, developed in detail by Knoppers in Anchor Bible 1 Chronicles 10-29 and by Sara Japhet in her OTL Chronicles commentary, is that this is a deliberate theological edit by the Chronicler. Peggy Day's groundbreaking work An Adversary in Heaven shows that in the Hebrew Bible "satan" begins as a generic noun (the adversary, a role, often human) and only develops into a proper-name supernatural figure during the post-exilic period. 1 Chronicles 21:1 is widely cited as one of the earliest texts where "Satan" appears without the definite article — that is, no longer "the adversary" but "Satan" as a personal name. The Chronicler is doing theology by editing his source. He is solving the problem of God-causing-evil by introducing a new character to absorb the blame.

The verdict is that the contradiction is not just real — it is theologically load-bearing. It tells us that the Israelite conception of evil was evolving, that Satan as a personal supernatural agent is a late development in Hebrew thought, and that biblical writers felt free to revise their sources for theological reasons. That is not what an inerrant divinely-dictated text looks like. That is what a human religious tradition developing over centuries looks like.

contradictions.question: How many generations were between Levi and Moses?
contradictions.summary: Exodus 6:16-20 and 1 Chronicles 6:1-3 and 1 Chronicles 23:6-12 all give the same three-generation chain from Levi to Moses: Levi -> Kohath -> Amram -> Moses. Meanwhile 1 Chronicles 7:22-27 gives a parallel chain through Ephraim — son of Joseph, who was Levi's brother, both sons of Jacob — that includes ten generations down to Joshua. Moses and Joshua are contemporaries. Yet one line is three generations long and the other is ten, supposedly covering the same span of time.
contradictions.commentary:
This is a contradiction that traditional readers usually walk past, because it requires you to actually count carefully across two genealogies. Once you do, the problem is glaring. Exodus 12:40 says the Israelites were in Egypt for 430 years. If we trust the Levi-to-Moses chain in Exodus 6, then in 430 years there were only three generations — Kohath, Amram, Moses — averaging roughly 143 years per generation. That is biologically implausible even by ancient Near Eastern standards. Meanwhile the Ephraim-to-Joshua chain in 1 Chronicles 7:22-27 gives ten generations, averaging a much more realistic 43 years per generation.

The traditional apologetic move is to argue that the Levi-Moses chain is telescoped — that "Amram begat Moses" really means "Amram was the ancestor of Moses," with unnamed generations in between. Archer and Kenneth Kitchen both deploy this defense. There is some basis for it in ancient Near Eastern genealogical convention. The problem is that Numbers 3:27-28 and Numbers 26:58-59 explicitly count Amram's descendants — listing the Amramites as a Levitical clan — and Exodus 6:20 names Jochebed (Amram's wife) as Amram's father's sister, which only makes sense if Amram is directly the father of Moses. Telescoping doesn't square with the surrounding text that treats Amram as Moses' direct biological father.

The critical scholarship, including Knoppers in Anchor Bible 1 Chronicles 1-9 and William Propp in his Anchor Bible Exodus commentary, treats this as evidence that the Priestly source (P) which produced the Exodus 6 genealogy had a compressed schematic chronology that contradicts the longer chronological framework elsewhere in the Pentateuch. The P writer was constructing a tidy three-generation parallel between Levi and his sons and Moses' immediate family, prioritizing literary symmetry over chronological coherence. The Ephraim line in 1 Chronicles 7 preserves a separate, fuller tradition. Marshall Johnson's classic work The Purpose of the Biblical Genealogies works through dozens of such contradictions and shows that biblical genealogies were ideological constructions, not registry records.

The verdict is that the two genealogies cannot both be historically accurate. Either the Levi line is telescoped — in which case the explicit textual claims about Jochebed and the Amramite clan get awkward — or the Ephraim line is inflated. The simplest reading is that both lists are theological constructions serving different rhetorical purposes, and the chronological gap between them is the gap between two different scribal schools.

contradictions.question: Who were the sons of Heman?
contradictions.summary: 1 Chronicles 25:4 lists fourteen sons of Heman by name: Bukkiah, Mattaniah, Uzziel, Shebuel, Jerimoth, Hananiah, Hanani, Eliathah, Giddalti, Romamtiezer, Joshbekashah, Mallothi, Hothir, and Mahazioth. 2 Chronicles 29:14 names only two — Jehiel and Shimei — and includes neither of them in the Chronicler's longer fourteen-name list. Same Heman, supposedly the king's seer and chief Levitical musician, two completely non-overlapping rosters of his sons.
contradictions.commentary:
This one is interesting because both passages come from the same author — the Chronicler. He cannot keep his own genealogical records straight across a span of four chapters. The 1 Chronicles 25 list is widely recognized as having a numerical-acrostic structure: the names Giddalti, Romamtiezer, Joshbekashah, Mallothi, Hothir, and Mahazioth can be read as fragments of a Hebrew prayer when strung together. Some critical scholars, including Knoppers and Japhet, have argued that this list is a literary or liturgical construction, not a registry of biological sons.

The apologist harmonization is the standard "different Heman" move — that the Heman of 1 Chronicles 25 (the Levite musician, son of Joel, descendant of Kohath) is a different Heman from the one in 2 Chronicles 29:14 whose sons assist in Hezekiah's temple purification. That is possible in principle, since Heman is a generic name. The problem is that 2 Chronicles 29:14 explicitly identifies Jehiel and Shimei as "the sons of Heman" in a list of Levitical singers participating in temple work — exactly the function of the Heman in 1 Chronicles 25. The contextual identification is the same. The second harmonization — that the lists are partial and we should just assume Jehiel and Shimei were among Heman's other unlisted sons — runs into the wall of 1 Chronicles 25:5, which explicitly says God gave Heman "fourteen sons and three daughters." Fourteen. A count. And neither Jehiel nor Shimei is named.

The critical reading, articulated by Knoppers in Anchor Bible 1 Chronicles 10-29 and by Ralph Klein in Hermeneia 2 Chronicles, is that the Chronicler is working with at least two separate Levitical-singer traditions and has not harmonized them. The 1 Chronicles 25 list with its embedded prayer-acrostic looks like a stylized literary construction. The 2 Chronicles 29 list looks like an independent tradition of which Levitical musicians were active under Hezekiah. The Chronicler preserved both without reconciling them.

The verdict is straightforward. One author, two lists of the same man's sons, no overlap and an explicit count of fourteen that doesn't include the two named elsewhere. The harmonization requires positing either a different Heman with no textual support or partial lists that contradict the Chronicler's own count.

contradictions.question: Was Asa perfect?
contradictions.summary: 1 Kings 15:14 and 2 Chronicles 15:17 both declare that "the heart of Asa was perfect with the Lord all his days." 2 Chronicles 16:7-10 then narrates Asa relying on the king of Syria instead of Yahweh, being rebuked by the prophet Hanani, throwing the prophet in prison, and "oppressing some of the people" in his rage. Either his heart was perfect with the Lord all his days, or he committed impieties severe enough to warrant prophetic condemnation in those same days.
contradictions.commentary:
What makes this contradiction especially sharp is that it lives inside a single book. 2 Chronicles 15:17 says Asa's heart was perfect all his days; 2 Chronicles 16 then describes him being faithless, imprisoning a prophet, and being struck with a foot disease in his last years that the Chronicler explicitly frames as divine punishment. The Chronicler is the source of both statements. He is contradicting himself one chapter apart.

The apologist harmonization, advanced by Archer and Walter Kaiser, is that "perfect" (Hebrew shalem) doesn't mean morally flawless — it means "wholly devoted," indicating overall loyalty to Yahweh rather than sinless behavior. The argument is that Asa's general direction was faithful even though he had specific lapses. That is actually a defensible reading of shalem in some contexts. The word can mean "complete" or "undivided" rather than "perfect" in the modern moral sense. The NRSV reasonably translates it as "true." The problem is that 1 Kings 15:14 and 2 Chronicles 15:17 explicitly extend this "perfect/true heart" qualifier across "all his days." Not most of his days. Not his early years. All of them. And 2 Chronicles 16:7-12 describes specific actions that the Chronicler himself frames as Asa failing to rely on Yahweh — which is exactly the disposition the "perfect heart" language is supposed to describe.

The critical reading, found in Sara Japhet's OTL Chronicles commentary and in Raymond Dillard's Word Biblical Commentary 2 Chronicles, is that the Chronicler is working with two sources or theological frames that he has not fully reconciled. The general regnal evaluation formula ("his heart was true all his days") is a stock Deuteronomistic-style summary borrowed from the source material in 1 Kings 15. The narrative of Asa's later failure with Hanani and the foot disease is the Chronicler's own theological elaboration — part of his characteristic pattern of showing kings who start well and end badly as a warning to his post-exilic audience. The two sections were written for different rhetorical purposes and the Chronicler did not bother to soften the seam between them.

The verdict is that the Chronicler is contradicting himself within a single narrative because he is splicing source material and theological commentary together. The harmonization works only if "all his days" doesn't actually mean all his days, at which point you've drained the word "perfect" of any real content. The plain reading of both passages cannot be made consistent.

contradictions.question: Who was Zechariah's father?
contradictions.summary: 2 Chronicles 24:20-21 narrates the stoning of Zechariah son of Jehoiada "in the court of the house of the Lord" — exactly the death scenario Jesus references in Matthew 23:35. But Matthew calls the victim "Zacharias son of Barachias." So either Jesus (or Matthew) has the wrong father's name for the high-profile temple-court murder, or the Gospel is referring to a different Zechariah entirely.
contradictions.commentary:
This contradiction has bothered Christian commentators since antiquity. Jerome already noted the problem in the fourth century. The scenario Jesus describes — a Zechariah murdered between the temple and the altar — fits 2 Chronicles 24 exactly. That is the only canonical Hebrew Bible account of a priest-prophet being killed in the temple courtyard. The problem is that the 2 Chronicles Zechariah is the son of Jehoiada, while Matthew's Zechariah is the son of Barachias.

The apologist harmonization branches into several attempts. Archer's main move is to argue that Jehoiada had two names — Jehoiada and Barachias — or that Barachias was Jehoiada's father, making Jehoiada the grandfather rather than the father of this Zechariah, and Matthew is using "son of" in the looser ancestral sense. There is zero textual evidence for any of this. The 2 Chronicles narrative names only Jehoiada as Zechariah's father, and the Hebrew Bible elsewhere never refers to Jehoiada as Barachias or vice versa. A second harmonization, advanced by some traditional commentators, is that Jesus is referring to Zechariah the prophet (the post-exilic prophet of the book of Zechariah), whose father was Berechiah (Zechariah 1:1). That is a closer name match, but Zechariah the prophet was not murdered in the temple — there is no biblical or extra-biblical record of his death by stoning. So this harmonization rescues the name at the cost of breaking the death scenario.

The critical reading, developed in detail by Davies and Allison in their ICC Matthew and by Raymond Brown in The Death of the Messiah, is that Matthew has confused or conflated two Zechariahs. The author of Matthew was working with the figure from 2 Chronicles (whose death scenario Jesus references) but supplied the wrong patronymic — possibly cross-pollinating from Zechariah the prophet, or from Zechariah son of Baris, an eminent citizen murdered by Zealots in the temple courts during the Jewish War (Josephus, War 4.335-344, c. 67-68 CE). Several critical scholars including Dale Allison have noted that the Josephus parallel is striking enough that Matthew may even be reading Christian persecution backwards into Jesus' speech. Whatever the source of the confusion, the simplest explanation is that the author of Matthew got the patronymic wrong.

The verdict is that the contradiction is real and the harmonizations are post-hoc patches. Either Matthew has erred on the patronymic, or Jesus is referring to a temple-courtyard murder we have no other record of involving a Barachias-fathered Zechariah, which is a counsel of desperation. The cleanest reading is that the Gospel writer confused two figures named Zechariah — a perfectly normal mistake for any human author working without access to a unified database of biblical priests.

contradictions.question: Where did Josiah die?
contradictions.summary: 2 Kings 23:29-30 says Pharaoh Necho slew king Josiah at Megiddo, and his servants "carried him in a chariot dead from Megiddo" and brought the body to Jerusalem. 2 Chronicles 35:23-24 instead says Josiah was wounded by archers at Megiddo, was brought back alive to Jerusalem, and "died" there. Same king, same battle, but Kings has him dead at Megiddo while Chronicles has him dying in Jerusalem.
contradictions.commentary:
Both accounts agree that Josiah was wounded at Megiddo fighting Necho's Egyptian forces around 609 BCE — this is one of the few biblical events with reasonable external Near Eastern documentation. The disagreement is about where he died. Kings says Megiddo, Chronicles says Jerusalem.

The apologist harmonization is well-rehearsed. Archer and Walter Kaiser argue that Kings is using "slew" in a loose proleptic sense — Necho effectively killed him at Megiddo by inflicting the mortal wound, and the body being carried "dead from Megiddo" is shorthand for being carried mortally wounded from Megiddo. Kings is summarizing; Chronicles is giving the detailed account. That is one way to read it, and the verb hemit ("caused to die" / "killed") in the Hiphil can occasionally have causative-by-mortal-wound force. The problem is that 2 Kings 23:30 specifically says his servants "carried him in a chariot dead from Megiddo" — the word is met, "dead," not "dying." Hebrew has a perfectly good word for dying-but-not-yet-dead (gowea), and Kings does not use it. The text says he was dead when they put him in the chariot.

The critical reading, articulated by Cogan and Tadmor in Anchor Bible II Kings and by Sara Japhet in her OTL Chronicles, is that the Chronicler has expanded and modified the Kings account for theological purposes. The Chronicler systematically reworks Kings to fit a tighter retribution theology — kings who die badly must die for specific reasons, and Josiah's death needs explanation because Kings has just declared him the most righteous king in Judah's history. So the Chronicler invents (or imports from elsewhere) the detail that Josiah disregarded Necho's warning from God (2 Chronicles 35:21-22), and the dying-in-Jerusalem scenario gives Josiah time to be properly mourned. Christopher Begg's work on the Chronicler's source-handling, published across several CBQ and ETL articles, documents this pattern extensively.

The verdict is that the harmonization works only if you stretch "dead" in 2 Kings 23:30 to mean "dying." The Chronicler is expanding his source for theological reasons, not preserving an independent eyewitness tradition. Either Kings has it right and Josiah was already dead when they removed him from the battlefield, or Chronicles has it right and he lingered until Jerusalem. The texts cannot both be plainly accurate without doing violence to the Hebrew of 2 Kings.

contradictions.question: Did Jehoiakim die in Babylon or near Jerusalem?
contradictions.summary: 2 Chronicles 36:5-6 says Nebuchadnezzar bound Jehoiakim in fetters "to carry him to Babylon." Jeremiah 22:18-19 prophesies that Jehoiakim will receive the burial of an ass and be "cast forth beyond the gates of Jerusalem." The implication of Chronicles is that he was carried off to Babylon; Jeremiah specifies an ignominious burial just outside Jerusalem. Both passages cannot be plainly accurate without rewriting one of them.
contradictions.commentary:
What makes this contradiction particularly thorny is that even the historical record outside the Bible is unclear about how Jehoiakim died. 2 Kings 24:6 says only that "Jehoiakim slept with his fathers" — the standard biblical euphemism for peaceful death and burial — and gives no location. The Babylonian Chronicle for Nebuchadnezzar's reign confirms an attack on Judah around 598 BCE but does not specify Jehoiakim's fate. So we are working with three biblical traditions and external silence, and the three biblical traditions don't agree.

The apologist harmonization, advanced by Archer and Kaiser, is to argue that 2 Chronicles only describes Nebuchadnezzar's intent to take Jehoiakim to Babylon, not that the trip was completed. The Hebrew laholikho babelah ("to bring him to Babylon") is an infinitive expressing purpose — Nebuchadnezzar bound him intending to deport him but Jehoiakim died en route or in Jerusalem before deportation occurred. That is actually a defensible reading of the syntax. The infinitive construct can express purpose. But the Chronicler's narrative goes on to describe other temple vessels being carried off to Babylon in the next breath, framing Jehoiakim as part of the same general deportation event. The reader is left with the impression that he ended up in Babylon, even if the grammar formally leaves it open.

The critical reading, found in Cogan and Tadmor's Anchor Bible II Kings (working from the Kings parallel), and developed for Chronicles by Sara Japhet and Ralph Klein, treats the three accounts as preserving divergent traditions about how a Judahite king who resisted Babylonian power died. Lundbom in his Anchor Bible Jeremiah notes that the Jeremiah 22:18-19 prophecy is harsh and probably reflects either an actual ignominious death or a piece of prophetic invective that did not literally come to pass (the Hebrew Bible is full of unfulfilled prophecies, despite traditional claims otherwise). The Chronicler, writing centuries later, smoothed over the harsh Jeremiah tradition by replacing the disgraceful burial with a vaguer fetters-and-deportation scenario. 2 Kings split the difference with the formulaic "slept with his fathers," which usually implies peaceful succession.

The verdict is that we have three different biblical pictures and no way to reconcile them without straining one or another. The harmonization that Chronicles only describes Nebuchadnezzar's intent is grammatically possible but contextually weak. The simplest reading is that different biblical writers preserved different traditions about a king whose death was, evidently, not well-remembered. That is a perfectly human explanation for the kind of textual divergence we actually see.

contradictions.question: How many of Arah's offspring returned from Babylon?
contradictions.summary: Ezra 2:5 says the children of Arah who returned from Babylonian exile numbered 775. Nehemiah 7:10 — giving the same census of returnees from the same family — says 652. Same family, same return, two different population counts that differ by 123 men.
contradictions.commentary:
Ezra 2 and Nehemiah 7 are parallel lists of the families who returned from exile under Cyrus' decree. They are duplicate documents — one of them is copied or adapted from the other, or both are drawn from a common archival source. So when they disagree on numbers, the disagreement is between two copies of essentially the same census record. And they disagree on numbers a lot — this is just one of about twenty cases where the totals for individual families differ between Ezra 2 and Nehemiah 7.

The apologist harmonization, advanced by Archer and elaborated by John W. Haley in his nineteenth-century classic Alleged Discrepancies, is that the two lists were taken at different times. Ezra 2 records the count at the time of registration in Babylon before the journey, while Nehemiah 7 records the count after arrival in Jerusalem — with the differences explained by deaths during travel, people who joined the caravan late, people who turned back, etc. That is a tidy theory. The problem is that both texts explicitly say they are listing the people who came up from the captivity to Jerusalem. Ezra 2:1: "these are the children of the province that went up out of the captivity... and came again unto Jerusalem." Nehemiah 7:6: "these are the children of the province, that went up out of the captivity... and came again to Jerusalem." Same description. Both are post-arrival lists, on their own framing.

The critical reading, found in Hugh Williamson's Word Biblical Commentary on Ezra-Nehemiah and in Joseph Blenkinsopp's OTL Ezra-Nehemiah, treats this as classic textual transmission divergence between two copies of the same source document. The numerical discrepancies between Ezra 2 and Nehemiah 7 are systematic across the list, but the family names and order are essentially identical, indicating a common Vorlage. Numerals in pre-exilic and early Persian Hebrew were often written using single-letter abbreviations or visually similar characters, and number corruption is among the most common transmission errors. The totals at the end of both lists actually agree (42,360), even though the individual sub-totals don't add up to that figure in either book — meaning the round total is from one tradition while the individual numbers have drifted in the copying.

The verdict is that the harmonization requires inventing a registration-versus-arrival distinction that the texts themselves contradict. The transmission-error reading explains both the systematic divergence in individual numbers and the agreement in the round total. Either way, the texts cannot both be plainly accurate without doing serious violence to one of them.

contradictions.question: How many of Pahathmoab, Jeshua, and Joab's offspring returned from Babylon?
contradictions.summary: Ezra 2:6 counts the descendants of Pahath-moab through Jeshua and Joab who returned from exile as 2,812. Nehemiah 7:11 — listing the same family from the same return — gives 2,818. The two parallel registers differ by six men for this family alone.
contradictions.commentary:
This is one in a long series of small numerical discrepancies between the parallel returnee lists in Ezra 2 and Nehemiah 7. Within the same chapter pair you can find divergences of zero, one, two, six, twenty-three, fifty, ninety, even hundreds, with the Pahath-moab figure landing at six. The pattern itself is the evidence.

The Archer-Haley harmonization here is the same as for entry 318 — that the lists were taken at different times, with Ezra reflecting a count at one point and Nehemiah another. That theory has the same problem we already worked through: both texts describe themselves as recording the people who actually returned to Jerusalem, not partial registers from different dates. Adding the extra timing-distinction is post-hoc rationalization that the texts do not support.

The critical reading, articulated by Williamson in WBC Ezra-Nehemiah and by Blenkinsopp in OTL Ezra-Nehemiah, is that these are two copies of essentially the same source document — likely a Persian-period archival census of returnees from Babylon — with numerical drift between them caused by scribal transmission. Loring Batten's older ICC commentary on Ezra-Nehemiah catalogued every discrepancy between the lists and showed the pattern is non-systematic: some numbers in Ezra are higher, some in Nehemiah are higher, the differences range from one to several hundred. That is exactly the random walk you would expect from scribal copying of numeric data over generations. Ralph Klein's monograph Textual Criticism of the Old Testament documents how Hebrew numerical notation systems were vulnerable to corruption, especially when small letter-strokes could change one digit to another.

The verdict is that the cleanest reading is unsexy but accurate: a Persian-period archival document was copied multiple times, with small numerical errors accumulating in each transmission line, and the canon preserved both downstream versions side by side. The texts cannot both be accurate at the level of plain reading. The harmonization requires inventing a different-time-of-census distinction that the texts themselves rule out. The contradiction is small but it is real, and the pattern across the full list rules out coincidence.

contradictions.question: How many of Zattu's offspring returned from Babylon?
contradictions.summary: Ezra 2:8 puts the children of Zattu who returned from Babylonian exile at 945. Nehemiah 7:13 — counting the same family in the same parallel list — says 845. A clean one-hundred-man discrepancy in two passages that are otherwise reporting identical material.
contradictions.commentary:
This is the third Ezra/Nehemiah parallel-list discrepancy in this batch, and the 100-man gap on Zattu is one of the larger individual divergences in the dataset. When the same author or editorial circle is preserving two copies of the same census and they disagree this consistently, the inerrancy claim takes serious damage.

The apologist response is the now-familiar Archer harmonization — different counts at different times, registration versus arrival, deaths in transit, late additions. Ralph Klein and Hugh Williamson both note that this defense fails for the same reasons we worked through on entries 318 and 319. Both lists frame themselves as registers of those who actually arrived in Jerusalem. Both lists give the same round total (42,360). The differences are not concentrated in a way that fits any narrative — they are scattered randomly across the families, which is exactly what scribal-error transmission looks like and is exactly what a coherent two-different-occasions theory would not predict.

A more sophisticated apologetic move, advanced by Edwin Yamauchi in his Ezra-Nehemiah commentary, is to grant that the numbers are textually corrupted but argue this is a minor matter that does not affect the historical reliability of the lists overall. That is actually a reasonable concession — but it concedes the contradiction. Once you grant that the numbers are corrupted in transmission, you have abandoned the inerrancy claim for these specific numbers. You have agreed with the critical scholars. The only remaining question is whether you call the corruption a "contradiction" or a "transmission variant." The phenomenon is the same. Two copies of the same source document, in the same canonical Bible, give different numbers, and at least one of them is wrong.

The verdict is the same as the other Ezra/Nehemiah pairings. The parsimonious explanation is that the Persian-period archival census was copied through multiple manuscript lines, and the resulting numerical variants got preserved in both Ezra and Nehemiah. The harmonization requires either inventing a registration/arrival distinction the texts deny, or conceding that the numbers are corrupted — at which point you have already agreed with the textual critics.
